title: Project 3: student record manager
learningObjectives: Define a Student structure that groups an ID, a bounded name and marks into one record.
Explain how an array of structures and a separate count represent a bounded collection.
Implement add and search operations while enforcing positive, unique student IDs.
Update a record and delete it safely by shifting later array elements.
Validate line-based input, integer IDs, names and finite marks before changing stored data.
Test normal operations, duplicate IDs, missing records, invalid values and full capacity.

understand.concept: A student record manager keeps related fields together in a structure. This version uses struct Student with a positive integer ID, a fixed-size character array for the name and a double for marks. An array stores up to 100 records; a separate size_t count tells the program how many array elements are currently active. The project is intentionally in-memory: records disappear when the program exits. File persistence is handled in a later project.
understand.whyItMatters: Record-oriented programs are common in schools, shops and offices. This project combines structures, arrays, functions, searching, validation and menu-driven control flow without hiding the data model behind a library.
understand.analogy: Think of each structure as one paper student card and the array as a bounded stack of cards. The count identifies how many cards are currently in use.
understand.analogyLimit: C does not automatically check array capacity or string length. The program must enforce those limits before writing to an element or copying text.

explain.narrative:
Start by defining the record layout, then decide the collection limit and the meaning of count. Only elements from index 0 through count - 1 are active. Never read an unused array element. Before adding, reject a full collection, invalid fields and an ID already present. A linear search is appropriate for this small unsorted collection; it returns count as a not-found sentinel because count is outside the active index range.

For an update, locate the record first and validate the replacement value before changing it. For deletion, shift each later active record one position to the left, then decrement count. The old final slot is no longer active and must not be included in listings.

Use fgets for complete lines, then parse numbers with strtol or strtod. Check conversion errors, trailing non-whitespace characters and domain limits. A name may contain spaces, must not be empty, and must fit in its destination array including the terminating null character. Reject overlong input rather than silently storing a truncated name.

This example stores marks from 0 through 100 and IDs from 1 through INT_MAX. It does not write files or claim that the data survives a restart. A later file-based project can add persistence after the in-memory operations are reliable.

examples.title: Testable record operations: add, find, update and delete
examples.explanation: The first program isolates collection operations from user input. Assertions verify successful additions, duplicate rejection, capacity limits, search results, a valid update, an invalid mark and deletion by shifting. The small capacity of three makes the full-storage boundary easy to test.

examples.title: Complete menu-driven student record manager
examples.explanation: The second program provides add, list, search, update and delete menu actions. It accepts names with spaces, checks numeric conversions and field ranges, rejects duplicate IDs and overlong lines, and exits cleanly on EOF. It stores at most 100 records in memory; no file persistence is attempted.

practise.guidedTask: Trace the deterministic example. Add the three valid records, identify why the duplicate and fourth record are rejected, update Ravi's marks, then delete Asha. Draw the array before and after deletion and explain why count changes from three to two.
practise.independentTask: Extend the interactive manager with a validated option to update a student's name as well as marks. Keep the same fixed capacity and unique-ID rule. Test blank names, names that exceed the buffer, duplicate IDs, marks below 0 or above 100, malformed numeric text, a missing ID, deletion from the first/middle/last position and an empty list. Do not add file storage in this project.
hints: Use one struct Student definition so every record has the same field layout.
Keep count separate from the array capacity; only indices smaller than count contain active records.
Search linearly and return count when an ID is not found.
Check for duplicate IDs before copying a new structure into the array.
When deleting, shift only active elements and decrement count exactly once.
Read a full line with fgets, parse with strtol or strtod, and reject trailing text, overflow and out-of-range values.

questions.prompt: What does count represent in the fixed-size student array?
options: The number of active records stored in the array.
The maximum number of bytes in a name.
The ID of the last student.
questions.answer: The number of active records stored in the array.
questions.explanation: The capacity is the array's fixed maximum; count tracks how many elements are currently active.

questions.prompt: Why should the program check for an existing ID before adding a record?
options: To enforce the rule that each student ID is unique.
To make the array grow automatically.
questions.answer: To enforce the rule that each student ID is unique.
questions.explanation: A duplicate check prevents two records from representing the same student identifier.

questions.prompt: If find_student returns count, what does that mean?
options: The requested ID was not found in the active records.
The array is guaranteed to be full.
The student is stored at index count.
questions.answer: The requested ID was not found in the active records.
questions.explanation: Valid active indices range from zero to count minus one, so count is a safe not-found sentinel.

questions.prompt: What must happen after deleting a record from the middle of the array?
options: Shift later active records left and decrement count.
Increase count and leave a gap.
Clear the entire array and restart.
questions.answer: Shift later active records left and decrement count.
questions.explanation: Shifting preserves a contiguous active range, and decrementing count removes the former final element from that range.

questions.prompt: Which input strategy best protects the name field from overflow?
options: Read a bounded line, check its length and copy only when it fits.
Use gets and assume the user enters a short name.
Copy input without checking its length.
questions.answer: Read a bounded line, check its length and copy only when it fits.
questions.explanation: Bounded input and an explicit length check protect the destination array and preserve its null terminator.
